justice: The lane is dominated by a single narrow carriageway, while the pedestrian space is reduced to a very thin strip of paving along the left edge, indicating limited spatial allocation for non-motorized users.
Cars parked directly along the right wall occupy part of the already narrow street section, reinforcing priority for vehicle storage over shared public access.
No visible curb ramps, tactile paving, or marked accessible crossing facilities are present, so barrier-free access is weak for the full range of road users.
The long blank wall on the right and gated frontage on the left provide little public interface or inclusive street amenities, suggesting low fairness in how the street serves different user needs.
safety: The roadway is extremely narrow, so pedestrians, cyclists, and cars would have to share the same constrained space, increasing conflict risk.
Parked cars on the right side further pinch the travel width, creating visibility and passing hazards for both drivers and walkers.
There are no visible sidewalks with protective separation, bike lanes, crosswalks, bollards, or traffic-calming markings to organize movement safely.
Overhead utility wires and an enclosed alley-like form, combined with limited visible lighting infrastructure, may reduce perceived safety, especially in low-light conditions.
livability: The street lacks visible shops, seating, community facilities, or active ground-floor uses, so it appears to offer little support for daily social life.
Blank walls and barred windows create a closed environment with limited street interaction, reducing neighborhood vibrancy.
The lane appears functional mainly for access rather than lingering, with no evident public gathering space, planting zone, or recreational element.
Very limited visible pedestrian activity and inactive facades suggest low everyday street vitality.
sustainability: There is almost no street tree canopy or continuous green infrastructure, aside from sparse vegetation climbing on the right-side structure.
No visible bike lane, bike parking, bus stop, or transit-related element supports low-carbon travel choices on this street.
The surface appears largely hard-paved with minimal permeable landscape area, and no rain garden, swale, or drainage feature is apparent.
On-street car parking in a narrow lane encourages car presence without corresponding sustainable mobility infrastructure.
aesthetics: The white walls and traditional low-rise building forms provide some visual coherence along the lane.
However, the long blank wall on the right and barred, weathered facades on the left create a stark and monotonous streetscape.
Overhead utility wires and exposed building attachments add visual clutter to the sky view.
Limited greenery and a lack of decorative street elements reduce overall visual appeal despite some historic character in the built form.
comfort: There is little visible tree shade or purpose-built shelter, so thermal comfort would be weak during hot or rainy weather.
No benches, ledges for resting, or other street furniture are visible, limiting physical comfort for people who may need to pause.
The very narrow walking edge beside moving or parked vehicles can create psychological discomfort because pedestrians have minimal refuge space.
The pavement looks mostly level and smooth in the carriageway, but the pedestrian strip is narrow and constrained by building edges.
walkability: A continuous, standard-width sidewalk is not present; instead, pedestrians appear limited to a very narrow edge strip on the left side.
The narrow lane forces walking close to vehicles and parked cars, reducing comfort and safety for routine pedestrian travel.
There are no visible crossings, curb extensions, wayfinding signs, or pedestrian-priority markings to support walking routes.
Inactive frontages, blank walls, and limited shade make the street less attractive for optional walking beyond basic access.
bikeability: The street has no visible bike lane, shared-lane marking, or cycling signage to indicate support for cyclists.
The narrow carriageway is further constrained by parked cars, leaving little safe operating space for bicycle passing or meeting traffic.
No bicycle parking racks or other cycling facilities are visible along the corridor.
The enclosed lane geometry and potential conflicts with cars emerging from or passing through the narrow corridor reduce cycling comfort and feasibility.
